extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of what propositions mean and what they assert (the matter of fact signified), including competing theories of predication, the role of names' connotation vs denotation, and a five-fold classification of matters-of-fact asserted by propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of belief in a proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate not the act of judgment but the thing believed: what is the immediate object of belief in a proposition, the matter of fact signified by it, and what is it to which assent is given?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or analyzing a proposition, focus on the proposition's content (the fact or phenomenon it asserts) rather than on the psychological act of believing; ask what fact (phenomenon, sequence, co-existence, existence, causation, resemblance) the proposition is intended to communicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes's theory of predication (names as co-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a proposition what is signified is the speaker's belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name; the proposition is true if both names are names of the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account explains predication only when both subject and predicate are proper names (e.g., 'Hyde was Clarendon'); it fails for general/connotative terms because it ignores connotation. It renders truth apparently arbitrary (dependent on naming) and is therefore inadequate as a general theory of predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names vs connotative (general) names: meaning resides in connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for proper names and some abstract names, the meaning of names resides in their connotation (the attributes they signify) rather than merely in what they denote (the individuals they name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general predicates evaluate the attributes connoted by the terms (e.g., 'man' connotes certain attributes; 'mortal' connotes the attribute of eventual death). Predication asserts that the attributes connoted by the predicate accompany those connoted by the subject. Examples: 'All men are mortal' asserts that the attributes connoted by 'man' are always accompanied by those connoted by 'mortal'; the combustibility of diamond was discovered empirically, not by an analysis of names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication as class membership (placing under a class)
rubrics_metrics.description: A widely held view: predication consists in referring something to a class—placing an individual under a class or placing one class under another (e.g., 'Man is mortal' = class man included in class mortal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account is closely related to the nominalist view but must be treated critically: classes are not preexisting fixed lists of individuals; they are determined by shared attributes. Use class-membership language with awareness that class-concepts often follow from, not precede, the acts of judgment that identify shared attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error of explaining classification by a posterior effect (ὕστερον προτέρον)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common logical error is to explain the origin of a judgment (or classification) by something that presupposes that judgment—i.e., to treat classification as prior when it is in many cases a concept that arises after repeated judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyses that assume classes were created by listing individuals; recognize that concepts of classes often develop after experiences and judgments about individuals. When assessing theories of predication, check whether they illegitimately presuppose the result they aim to explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence asserted in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: One fundamental kind of matter-of-fact a proposition can assert is simple existence (that some noumenon, phenomenon, or thing exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify propositions that assert mere existence (e.g., asserting that a noumenon or phenomenon exists) and distinguish these from claims about relations (co-existence, sequence, causation, resemblance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existence (Order in Time and Order in Place / Co-inherence of attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of co-existence assert that two phenomena occur together (co-existence) or that items occupy a relation in place (order in place); a special kind is co-inherence—the concurrence of attributes/functions in the same part or locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a co-existence claim, decide whether it is an order-in-place (spatial arrangement) or co-inherence (attributes/functional concurrence). Note co-inherence may be potential (attribute regarded as present even if not presently sensed, e.g., snow is white in darkness). Examples: physical properties co-inhering in substance (gold's lustre, hardness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence (Order in Time) asserted by propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions can assert sequence—that one phenomenon follows another in time (order in time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sequence claims from co-existence; sequence asserts temporal succession (e.g., claiming an effect occurs after a cause). Analyze temporal scope — propositions may only assert that something occurs 'at some time' rather than specifying when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation asserted in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions assert causation (that one thing is the cause of another); asserting existence of an unknown cause (noumenon) is an assertion of causation in another form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat causal claims as a distinct category of matter-of-fact. Remember assertions about substances or noumena (things-in-themselves) are grounded in phenomena and amount to causal claims about what produces observable phenomena. Reserve special scrutiny for causal inferences, which will be further discussed in later treatments (Third Book reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance as a kind of matter-of-fact
rubrics_metrics.description: A fifth kind of assertion is resemblance: propositions that assert that one phenomenon resembles another (e.g., colors resembling one another; 'this color is like that color').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that resemblance claims differ from sequence/co-existence; sometimes general predicates imply resemblance (class membership often grounded on resemblance), but many class-assertions properly assert possession of common attributes rather than mere resemblance. Some class-names (sensations) connote mere resemblance and thus when predicated convey likeness rather than analyzable attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between class-based assertions and resemblance-only cases
rubrics_metrics.description: While many general propositions refer to class-membership grounded in possession of specific attributes, there are cases where predicating a class-name affirms only resemblance (especially for classes of simple sensations or borderline taxa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating general predications, determine whether the predicate asserts possession of analyzable attributes or merely resemblance to other instances; watch for borderline cases where scientific significance of class-names is uncertain and careful qualification ('considered', 'may be ranked') is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms reducible to concrete terms
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract name is the name of an attribute; since the concrete general name connotes the attribute, any proposition expressed in abstract terms can be transformed into an equivalent proposition using concrete terms (the concrete names of the attributes or the phenomena grounding them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing abstract propositions, reduce them to concrete descriptions of the phenomena or attributes they denote to clarify their factual content; this aids in identifying which of the five kinds of matter-of-fact the proposition asserts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertions about substances/noumena are grounded in phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions about substances or noumena (things-in-themselves) are ultimately assertions concerning the phenomena by which those substances manifest themselves; statements about a noumenon presuppose and are grounded on observable phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with claims about underlying substances or 'things-in-themselves' (e.g., historical persons, unobservable entities), trace their foundation to the observable phenomena or series of facts that justify the assertion; be cautious about treating noumena as directly knowable apart from their phenomena.
